research_text:
## Research brief

### 1. Governed API and meaning of the reported condition

`java.security.KeyPairGenerator` is the JCA engine class for generating public/private key pairs for a selected algorithm. Instances are obtained through `getInstance`; they can then be initialized either with an algorithm-independent key size or with an algorithm-specific `AlgorithmParameterSpec`, and finally generate a `KeyPair`. The parameter-spec overloads accept a parameter set used to generate the keys.  
Source: Oracle Java SE API, <https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPairGenerator.html>. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPairGenerator.html))

The wording **“no preparation of the `AlgorithmParameterSpec` given to `KeyPairGenerator.initialize` was observed”** does **not** correspond to a JCA requirement that every parameter specification must have some generic “preparation” operation. In the cited CrySL file, it corresponds to the rule’s **required-predicate** conditions on the `params` variable when an `initialize(AlgorithmParameterSpec)` overload is used:

- RSA → `preparedRSA[params]`
- DSA → `preparedDSA[params]`
- Diffie-Hellman/DH → `preparedDH[params]`
- EC → `preparedEC[params]`

The rule source does not define what calls or provenance establish those predicates, nor does it contain the detector’s exact diagnostic message. Therefore, the source alone supports only the conclusion that the analysis did not establish the relevant named `prepared…[params]` predicate; it does **not** establish that the parameter set is invalid at runtime.  
Source: CrySL rule, <https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyPairGenerator.crysl>. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyPairGenerator.crysl))

### 2. Official JCA usage and documented remediation

Oracle documents two supported initialization forms:

1. **Algorithm-independent initialization** — `initialize(int keysize[, SecureRandom])`. The key size is an algorithm-specific measurement; absent further parameters, the provider selects algorithm-specific parameters. An unsupported size produces `InvalidParameterException`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPairGenerator.html))

2. **Algorithm-specific initialization** — `initialize(AlgorithmParameterSpec[, SecureRandom])`. The supplied `params` are the parameter set used to generate the keys. Inappropriate parameters produce `InvalidAlgorithmParameterException`; this overload can also fail with `UnsupportedOperationException` if the selected provider does not override the corresponding SPI method. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPairGenerator.html))

If the application performs no explicit initialization, Java requires each provider to supply and document a default initialization. However, Oracle explicitly warns that defaults can vary by provider and may change in a later version, and recommends **explicitly initializing the `KeyPairGenerator` rather than relying on provider-specific defaults**. That is the official documented remediation for reliance on defaults; it is not a blanket instruction to replace every key-size initialization with an `AlgorithmParameterSpec`.  
Source: <https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPairGenerator.html>. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPairGenerator.html))

Oracle also documents that general-purpose applications should normally not request a named JDK provider, because doing so couples the application to a provider that may be unavailable on other Java implementations and can prevent selection of a higher-priority optimized provider.  
Source: <https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/security/oracle-providers.html>. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/security/oracle-providers.html))

No invalid key-size conclusion can be drawn from this report without the actual algorithm, initialization overload, exact arguments, selected provider, and any runtime exception. Provider support differs. For example, the current Oracle-provider documentation lists SUN DSA support for multiples of 64 from 512 through 1024, plus 2048 and 3072; that is broader than the CrySL rule’s DSA constraint of `{3072}`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/security/oracle-providers.html))

### 3. Compatibility, formats, platform support, and migration

**Persisted and wire formats.** The `KeyPairGenerator` API documentation does not specify a persisted key format, a wire format, interoperability guarantees, or a migration procedure when initialization is changed. It only specifies generation and initialization behavior. Consequently, there is no documented `KeyPairGenerator`-level migration path for already persisted or transmitted keys in the reviewed sources. Any such compatibility question remains dependent on the separate key encoding, container, certificate, protocol, keystore, provider, and consumer APIs in use.

**Defaults and provider/version compatibility.** Oracle expressly documents that default initialization may vary among providers and that a provider’s default may change in a future version. Explicit initialization removes that particular default-selection variability, but Oracle does not promise that all parameter specifications are accepted by every provider. The parameter-spec initialization methods may reject inappropriate parameters, and provider SPI support may be absent. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPairGenerator.html))

**Platform version support.** The API class has existed since Java 1.1. The `initialize(int, SecureRandom)`, `initialize(AlgorithmParameterSpec)`, `initialize(AlgorithmParameterSpec, SecureRandom)`, and `genKeyPair()` documentation marks those methods as available since Java 1.2; the `getInstance(String, Provider)` overload is marked since Java 1.4. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPairGenerator.html))

For the currently reviewed Java SE 25 API, all platform implementations must support `DiffieHellman`, `DSA`, `EC`, `RSA`, `RSASSA-PSS`, and `X25519` `KeyPairGenerator` algorithms, with stated mandatory key sizes or curves. The standard-names specification separately lists additional standardized names such as EdDSA, XDH, ML-DSA, and ML-KEM, but implementation support beyond applicable platform requirements must be verified for the actual target JDK/provider.  
Sources: <https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPairGenerator.html> and <https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html>. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPairGenerator.html))

**Source limitation:** The reviewed official API and provider documentation does not identify the application’s JDK release, provider, parameter-spec subtype, stored-key encoding, or downstream protocol. It therefore cannot answer whether a particular change preserves an application’s persisted-data or wire compatibility.

### 4. Exact CrySL rule content and match scope

**Source examined:** `KeyPairGenerator.crysl` from the supplied repository URL:  
<https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyPairGenerator.crysl>

The specification header is, verbatim:

```text
SPEC java.security.KeyPairGenerator
```

The event declarations are, verbatim:

```text
EVENTS
	g1: getInstance(algorithm);
	g2: getInstance(algorithm, _);
	Get := g1 | g2;

	i1: initialize(keysize);
	i2: initialize(keysize, _);
	i3: initialize(params);
	i4: initialize(params, _);
	Init := i1 | i2 | i3 | i4;

	k1: keyPair = generateKeyPair();
	k2: keyPair = genKeyPair();
	Gen := k1 | k2;
```

The source declares these bound object types:

```text
java.lang.String algorithm;
java.security.KeyPair keyPair;
java.security.spec.AlgorithmParameterSpec params;
int keysize;
```

Thus, **the rule matches these method names and declared argument forms**:

| Event | Method names and argument forms |
|---|---|
| `Get` | `getInstance(algorithm)` or `getInstance(algorithm, _)` |
| `Init` | `initialize(keysize)`, `initialize(keysize, _)`, `initialize(params)`, or `initialize(params, _)` |
| `Gen` | `keyPair = generateKeyPair()` or `keyPair = genKeyPair()` |

The parameter list **is constrained at the event-declaration level**: one-argument and two-argument forms are separately listed; the first argument is bound either to `int keysize` or `AlgorithmParameterSpec params`; `_` is used for the unbound second argument. The source does not name the second argument’s type and does not impose a value constraint on it. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyPairGenerator.crysl))

The declared order is, verbatim:

```text
ORDER
	Get, Init, Gen
```

The rule then evaluates these constraints, verbatim:

```text
CONSTRAINTS
	algorithm in {"RSA", "EC", "DSA", "DiffieHellman", "DH"}; //BSI TR-02102-1 Recommends atleast 3000bits for keys
	algorithm in {"RSA"} => keysize in {4096, 3072};
	algorithm in {"DSA"} => keysize in {3072};
	algorithm in {"DiffieHellman", "DH"} => keysize in {3072};
	algorithm in {"EC"} => keysize in {256};
```

And it evaluates these required predicates, verbatim:

```text
REQUIRES
	algorithm in {"RSA"} => preparedRSA[params];
	algorithm in {"DSA"} => preparedDSA[params];
	algorithm in {"DiffieHellman", "DH"} => preparedDH[params];
	algorithm in {"EC"} => preparedEC[params];
```

Finally, the assurance declared by the file is:

```text
ENSURES
	generatedKeypair[keyPair, algorithm];
```

**Can it match a method merely because it shares an API method name?** **No such name-only matching rule is stated in this source.** The file scopes the specification to `SPEC java.security.KeyPairGenerator`; it does not state that a method on another receiver type is eligible merely because it is named `initialize`, `getInstance`, `generateKeyPair`, or `genKeyPair`. The file itself does not provide the CrySL/CryptoAnalysis implementation semantics needed to make a broader operational claim, but it provides no textual basis for name-only matching. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyPairGenerator.crysl))
